title: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
summary: Everything is made of particles. Learn to tell elements, compounds and mixtures apart, choose a separation technique, and explain states of matter and changes of state with the kinetic molecular model.

keyterms.definition: A substance made of only one type of atom, which cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means.
A substance of two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio, with properties different from its elements.
Two or more substances physically combined in no fixed ratio; each keeps its own properties and they can be separated physically.
A mixture with uniform composition and a single phase throughout, such as a solution or air.
A mixture whose composition is not uniform, with visibly different phases, such as sand in water.
Separating an insoluble solid from a liquid by passing the mixture through filter paper; the solid stays as the residue.
Separating liquids by boiling point: the more volatile component evaporates, then condenses and is collected.
Separating components by their different distribution between a stationary phase and a mobile phase.
Obtaining a solid solute by evaporating some solvent and cooling the saturated solution so crystals form.
Model in which matter consists of particles in constant random motion; their average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature.
Temperature scale starting at absolute zero; T/K = t/°C + 273.15. It is proportional to average particle kinetic energy.
Direct change of state from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state; the reverse is deposition.
A physical change between solid, liquid and gas in which intermolecular forces are overcome or formed at constant temperature.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a compound?
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride contains Na and Cl chemically combined in a fixed 1:1 ratio. Air and brass are mixtures; oxygen is an element.

questions.statement: The components of a mixture can be separated by physical methods.
questions.explanation: Components of a mixture are not chemically bonded, so filtration, distillation or chromatography can separate them.

questions.prompt: Which technique best separates ethanol (b.p. 78 °C) from water?
questions.explanation: Both are miscible liquids with different boiling points, so fractional distillation separates them: ethanol vaporizes first.

questions.text: Insoluble sand is removed from salt water by ___.
questions.explanation: Filtration retains the insoluble solid as residue while the solution passes through as filtrate.

questions.prompt: Salt water is best described as a…
questions.explanation: Dissolved salt is spread uniformly through one phase, so a solution is a homogeneous mixture.

questions.prompt: Match each mixture to the best separation technique.
questions.explanation: Choose the technique from the property that differs: solubility, boiling point or affinity for the phases.

questions.statement: A compound has the same properties as the elements it is made from.
questions.explanation: Chemical combination produces a new substance: sodium (reactive metal) and chlorine (toxic gas) form harmless table salt.

questions.text: In paper chromatography the solvent is the ___ phase.
questions.explanation: The solvent moves up the paper (mobile phase); the water held in the paper fibres is the stationary phase.

questions.prompt: Put the steps for obtaining pure salt crystals from rock salt in order.
items: Dissolve in warm water and stir
Evaporate some water from the filtrate
questions.explanation: Dissolving separates soluble salt from insoluble material; crystallizing the filtrate recovers the salt.
Oil and water form two separate layers (two phases), so the composition is not uniform.

lessons.title: States of matter and the kinetic model

options: The total energy of the particles
The average kinetic energy of the particles
The speed of the fastest particle
questions.explanation: Kelvin temperature is proportional to the average kinetic energy of the particles.

questions.statement: During melting of a pure solid the temperature stays constant.
questions.explanation: Energy supplied is used to overcome intermolecular forces (increase potential energy), not to raise the average kinetic energy.

questions.prompt: Solid iodine turning directly into a purple vapour is called…
questions.explanation: Solid → gas without a liquid stage is sublimation; gas → solid is deposition.

questions.prompt: Match each change of state to its name.
questions.explanation: Melting, vaporization and sublimation absorb energy; freezing, condensation and deposition release it.

questions.statement: Gas particles at the same temperature all move at the same speed.
questions.explanation: Particles have a range (distribution) of speeds; temperature relates to the average kinetic energy.

questions.prompt: Why is a gas much easier to compress than a liquid?
options: Gas particles are far apart with large spaces between them
questions.explanation: In a gas, particles are widely spaced, so the volume can be reduced by pushing them closer.

questions.text: Condensation is an ___ process because intermolecular forces form.
questions.explanation: Forming attractions between particles releases energy to the surroundings.

questions.prompt: A solid is heated steadily from below its melting point until it boils. Order the stages.
questions.explanation: A heating curve has sloping regions (kinetic energy rising) and flat plateaus (changes of state).

questions.prompt: Which state has particles in fixed positions that vibrate?
questions.explanation: In a solid, strong attractions hold particles in fixed positions; they can only vibrate.
